opus-5.5.text:
I think scaling had a very strong homogenizing effect, and it's worth being honest about that.

Before scaling became the dominant paradigm, research was quite exploratory. People tried all kinds of things, and the field didn't quite know what would work. Then a very clear recipe emerged: take a neural net, add more data and more compute, and it gets better. That recipe was incredibly powerful, and it was also very low-risk from an organizational point of view. If you're a company deciding where to put your resources, "scale up the thing that already works" is easy to justify. You don't need a new idea. You just need more GPUs.

So what happened is that scaling sucked a lot of the air out of the room. Everyone started doing roughly the same thing. You ended up in a situation where there are more companies than there are ideas, and I don't think that's an exaggeration. The word "scaling" itself became a kind of strategy, and it told people what to do. It made it harder to work on ideas that didn't fit neatly into it.

What's interesting is that we might now be moving back into an age of research, just with much bigger computers. Pre-training data is finite. At some point you can't keep getting the same returns from the same recipe, and you have to ask what you're actually scaling and whether it's the most productive use of compute. I think that question will bring back a lot of the diversity that was lost. Taste and good ideas will matter again in a way they arguably mattered less for a few years.

One more point. For research, you don't necessarily need the absolute maximum amount of compute to show that an idea is promising. Many of the most important breakthroughs were demonstrated on relatively modest hardware for their time. So the bottleneck for diversity was never only compute. It was also the incentive structure that scaling created. As that loosens, I expect we'll see far more variety in what people try.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling became the dominant paradigm and led everyone to do roughly the same thing.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says there are more companies than ideas.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I think the age of scaling had a very interesting effect, which is that it kind of sucked the air out of the room. Before, let's say, 2020 or so, if you were doing AI research, you had to have an idea. You had to think, what is the right architecture, what is the right objective, how should learning work. And people had lots of different ideas, and most of them didn't work, but the field was very diverse in what it was trying.

Then scaling came along, and it offered something very seductive, which is a recipe. You take the transformer, you take more data, you take more compute, and you get a better result. And it's low risk. If you're a researcher, or a company, and you have a recipe that reliably produces improvement, why would you go and do something weird that might not work? So everyone did the same thing. And it made sense. It was the rational thing to do. The scaling laws were real, and the results were real.

But the consequence is that the number of ideas being explored went down a lot. I would say the field became much less diverse intellectually, even as it became much larger in terms of people and money. You have many more researchers now, but they're mostly pushing on the same thing. And I think there's a certain irony there, because the idea that scaling works was itself a kind of insight. It was not obvious. But once it became obvious, it stopped being an idea and became an industry.

Now, I think we're at a point where this is changing. The easy scaling, in some sense, is becoming harder. The data is finite. The compute is enormous but it's not infinite, and the returns are not what they were. And so I think people are going to be forced to go back to having ideas again. Which I actually find quite exciting, because the question of how to learn, how to generalize, what intelligence really consists of, those questions were never fully answered. They were just postponed. And when you postpone a question for several years while everyone is doing the same thing, there is probably a lot of low-hanging fruit waiting for the people who go back and look.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling offered a reliable recipe and that researchers and companies consequently pursued the same approach, reducing the range of ideas explored.

r002.rationale: It says the field has many more researchers but less intellectual diversity; it does not state that AI companies substantially outnumber distinct ideas.

astra-6.text:
I think scaling has had this interesting effect where it gave everyone a very clear thing to do. You could take a fairly simple recipe, make it bigger, and get better results. And that was a tremendous discovery. But once that became clear, it also became harder to justify pursuing something very different. Why take a chance on an idea that might not work when you have something that you know will improve if you give it more compute?

So you get a concentration of effort. Different organizations, very talented people, working on fairly similar things. There is still ingenuity involved in making scaling work, but the overarching direction is shared.

I think as the returns to that approach become less predictable, you get more room for different ideas again. If the next step isn't obvious, people have to make different bets. And that's a very interesting situation for research.

r001.rationale: It says scaling offered a clear, reliable recipe and made different approaches harder to justify, concentrating organizations on similar research.

r002.rationale: It notes that different organizations pursue similar work, but does not state that AI companies substantially outnumber distinct ideas.

sol-6.1.text:
I think scaling has had two effects. On the one hand, it gave us something that works. That’s a very big deal. You could take a fairly simple idea, make the model bigger, give it more data and compute, and get substantially better results. So it was entirely reasonable for a lot of research to move in that direction.

But it also created a very strong incentive to pursue the same recipe. If you have a reliable way to make progress, it becomes harder to justify trying something very different, especially if the first experiments don’t work. And new ideas usually don’t work on the first try.

So I think the diversity of approaches probably decreased. But I wouldn’t equate that with a lack of creativity. There was a lot of ingenuity involved in making scaling work. The question is how much effort goes into improving the existing approach versus discovering the next one. When the returns from scaling become less straightforward, the incentive to explore becomes stronger again.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling provided a reliable path to progress and created a strong incentive to pursue the same recipe, reducing diversity of approaches.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare the number of AI companies with the number of distinct ideas.
